title: Tuga A6 vs Tuga W8: Pocket Android Scanner or Windows Tablet?
description: Tuga A6 (6 inch Android 15 handheld with a scanner, £349) or Tuga W8 (8 inch Windows 11 Pro tablet, £629)? £280 apart, and which job each one is for.
summary: The A6 is £280 cheaper, 277g against 750g, and has a Zebra 2D scan engine as standard; the W8 adds Windows 11 Pro, an 8 inch 700 nit screen, 8GB of RAM, USB-A, HDMI, a fingerprint sensor and MIL-STD-810G, with a scanner version at £699.
lede: For anyone weighing the cheapest scanning device in the range against a Windows tablet that can take a scanner. The short answer: buy the Tuga A6 at £349 if the job is scanning, photos and apps from a pocket, and the Tuga W8 at £629 (£699 with the 2D scanner) if you need a Windows program or a bigger screen in your hands.
verdict: These two are bought for different jobs, so start with the job. The Tuga A6 costs £349 and the Tuga W8 £629, a gap of £280, and the gap rises to £350 against the W8 with 2D Scanner at £699, which is the version to compare if scanning is why you are here. The A6 is a 6 inch Android 15 handheld at 277g with a Zebra 2D scan engine and two side scan keys built in as standard, sealed to IP67 and rated for 1.5 metre drops, with a removable 5050mAh battery. If the work is proof of delivery, stock checks, asset tags, job photos and messaging, and the apps for it run on Android or in a browser, the A6 does that from a pocket or a belt holster (£22) and leaves £280 or more in the bank.

The W8 is a different kind of device: an 8 inch Windows 11 Pro tablet at 750g, nearly three times the weight of the A6, with an Intel Celeron N5100, 8GB of RAM against 4GB and a 128GB SSD against 64GB. Its screen is bigger, 8 inches against 6, and rated at 700 nits, where the A6 lists no brightness figure, though the A6's 2160 x 1080 panel is sharper than the W8's 1280 x 800. The W8 has USB-C, USB-A and HDMI, a fingerprint sensor, a pogo pin dock connector and a MIL-STD-810G rating, and both are sealed to IP67. On the other side, the A6 is rated from -20°C to 50°C against -10°C to 50°C on the W8, its battery is removable where the W8's 5000mAh is not listed as removable, it lists a 1.5 metre drop rating where the W8 lists none, and it has a 13MP rear camera against 8MP and dual SIM 4G. The W8 does not list dimensions or a microSD slot; the A6 takes a microSD card up to 256GB.

Pay the £280 when one of three things is true: a program you rely on only installs on a Windows PC, you need USB-A or HDMI to plug into equipment or a screen, or a 6 inch screen is too small for the forms and drawings you work from. If you also scan, the W8 with 2D Scanner at £699 keeps the scanning on one device, at £350 over the A6. Check that your specific program runs on the W8 before you order; our Android or Windows guide has a five minute test for that. Both include the 12 month warranty, the paid 3-Year Warranty is £65 on the A6 and £79 on the W8, delivery is free to UK addresses in 7 to 10 working days, and there is no VAT to add to either price. For drivers and pickers, the logistics page shows where each one fits.
chooseA: The job is scanning, proof of delivery, photos and apps, and everything you use runs on Android or in a browser, so the W8's extras would be £280 spent on nothing you need.
You want the scanner built in at the lowest price: a Zebra 2D scan engine with two side scan keys at £349, against £699 for the W8 with 2D Scanner.
It has to live in a pocket or on a belt all day: 277g and 164 x 77.6 x 16mm, against 750g for the W8.
You want a removable battery: the A6's 5050mAh swaps for a charged spare, where the W8's 5000mAh is not listed as removable.
You want the listed drop rating and the wider cold rating: 1.5 metres and -20°C to 50°C on the A6, where the W8 lists no drop rating and -10°C to 50°C.
chooseB: One program you rely on only installs on a Windows PC, which settles it on its own, once you have checked it runs on the W8.
You plug into equipment or a screen: the W8 has USB-C, USB-A and HDMI, where the A6 has USB-C and charging contacts, with an £8 OTG adapter for USB-A devices.
You work from forms, drawings or spreadsheets that need an 8 inch screen rated at 700 nits, rather than 6 inches.
You want more memory and storage and a fingerprint sensor for sign-in: 8GB of RAM and a 128GB SSD against 4GB and 64GB, plus a fingerprint sensor the A6 does not have.
You want it docked at a desk or in the van: the Charging Dock (£49.99) and Vehicle Mounting Dock (£109) are listed for the W8, and no dock is listed for the A6.

faq.q: Is the Tuga W8 worth £280 more than the Tuga A6?
faq.a: Only if the job needs a Windows program, a bigger screen or the W8's ports. The W8 costs £629 and the A6 £349. What the £280 buys is Windows 11 Pro on an Intel Celeron N5100 with 8GB of RAM and a 128GB SSD, an 8 inch 700 nit screen, USB-A and HDMI, a fingerprint sensor and MIL-STD-810G. If you scan as well, the comparison is really with the W8 with 2D Scanner at £699, so the gap is £350. If your work runs on Android apps or in a browser, the Tuga A6 does it from a pocket with the scanner included. Both have the 12 month warranty, there is no VAT to add to either price, and delivery is free to UK addresses in 7 to 10 working days.

faq.q: Which is the better barcode scanner, the A6 or the W8 with 2D Scanner?
faq.a: Both have an integrated 2D scan engine; the difference is the device around it and the price. The A6's Zebra 2D scan engine sits in the top edge of a 277g handheld with two side scan keys that work with gloves on, at £349. The W8 with 2D Scanner puts a 2D scanner on a 750g 8 inch Windows tablet at £699, £70 over the standard W8 and £350 over the A6. For hundreds of scans a day on foot, the lighter one-handed device is the easier one to hold. If scans have to go straight into a Windows program, the W8 is the only one of the two that can run it. Test either with the labels you actually read, scuffed and in poor light, before you roll it out; our guide to built-in barcode scanners covers what to look for.

faq.q: Which is tougher, the A6 or the W8?
faq.a: They list different things. Both are sealed to IP67, which covers dust and immersion. The A6 lists a 1.5 metre drop rating and an operating range of -20°C to 50°C; the W8 lists no drop rating and -10°C to 50°C. The W8 lists MIL-STD-810G, which the A6 does not. So the A6 has the higher listed figures for drops and cold, and the W8 has the military standard rating. A 277g handheld also has less mass to land with than a 750g tablet. Our IP rating guide explains what IP67 is tested for, and our MIL-STD-810 guide covers what the military standard does and does not tell you.

The capacities are close, 5050mAh on the A6 and 5000mAh on the W8, but the A6 is running a 6 inch screen on a MediaTek Helio P35 and the W8 an 8 inch screen on an Intel Celeron N5100, so they will not last the same shift. The A6's battery is removable, so a charged spare can take over; the W8's is not listed as removable, though it lists fast charging. Spare batteries are not listed as an accessory for either, so ask us before you plan around one. For charging, the 12V DC Car Charger (£26) fits both, and the Charging Dock (£49.99) and Vehicle Mounting Dock (£109) are listed for the W8 only; see accessories. The A6 has charging contacts for a dock, but none is listed for it, so it charges over USB-C. Our guide to rugged tablets in cold weather explains what the cold does to any battery.
